first.rationale:
Two of the three current problems are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and simplify_onboarding is the one lever that plausibly addresses both at the same time without eroding price realization. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the obvious reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, but discount-led acquisition tends to buy exactly the price-sensitive, low-retention accounts that damage sustainable qualified revenue, and it does nothing for the two funnel declines. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are healthy directions but target segments that are not where the current bleed is. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the closest runner-up and remains the fallback if verification undercuts the onboarding record.

I am spending both verification pulls on the memories my chosen action actually rests on rather than on the tempting alternative: memory_31 and memory_86 are the entire evidentiary basis for simplify_onboarding, and both are old (day 12 and day 52) and consolidated into summary form. The specific thing I need from the archive is what outcome each experiment actually measured. Both summaries report proximal funnel metrics — completion rate, time-to-value, first-week activation — and neither claims a measured effect on downstream qualified revenue or retention. That gap is the central risk: cutting required signup fields reliably raises activation counts while degrading lead qualification, routing, and enrichment, so the funnel metric improves while revenue quality quietly falls. Note also that memory_57 is the only inherited record that explicitly checked for downstream harm ('without measurable harm to retention'), which suggests the others simply did not look rather than looked and found nothing.

So I am treating these memories as generally reliable about what they measured and genuinely uncertain about what they did not. I want to see, for memory_31, whether field removal was tested against lead quality or only signup conversion, and for memory_86, whether the 'durable' lift was tracked past week one. If the archive shows either was validated on revenue-quality outcomes, this scales up. If both were proximal-metric-only, I keep the direction but hold the guard rails.

Hence a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: limited traffic slice, holdout retained, and success judged on downstream qualified-revenue and retention proxies rather than on completion rate alone, which would otherwise be trivially easy to move in a way that flatters the experiment and hurts the objective.

final.rationale:
Verification largely resolved the risk I flagged, so I am upgrading from a small guarded test to a standard experiment — but not to broad rollout.

What the archive actually settled: exp_31 did measure a downstream outcome, and it was positive — qualified revenue +4% alongside signup +15% and activation +9%. That is the specific check I was worried was missing, and it came back clean. exp_86 measured 30-day retention at +3% with time-to-value down 2.1 days, which is the opposite of the 'proximal metric improves while quality decays' failure mode I was guarding against. Shortening the flow appears to genuinely deliver value faster rather than just pushing more bodies through a counter.

What remains unresolved, and why this is not a broad rollout. First, exp_31 carries an explicit non-replication note: it holds on SMB and did not replicate on other segments. Since the current bleed is concentrated in price-sensitive SMB accounts, that is fortunately the segment I care most about, but it means I cannot generalize the field-reduction result company-wide. Second, exp_31 showed 30-day retention at -1%. Small, plausibly noise, and outweighed by +4% qualified revenue — but it is directionally the exact erosion I predicted from looser qualification, so it deserves monitoring rather than dismissal. Third, exp_86 never measured revenue at all; its confirmation rests on completion, time-to-value, and retention. The two records are complementary rather than mutually confirming, and neither on its own establishes both halves of the case.

So: run onboarding simplification scoped to SMB self-serve, with a live holdout, judged primarily on qualified revenue and 30-day retention rather than completion rate — completion is too easy to move in ways that flatter the experiment. I am deliberately not taking the promotional_pricing bait despite the competitor's entry pricing; memory_73's acquisition-and-revenue framing says nothing about retention or margin on discount-acquired accounts, it is the one candidate whose downstream record I could not verify, and it addresses neither of the two funnel declines. Activation messaging (memory_91) stays queued as the next slot's candidate, since the -6% activation gap may not fully close from onboarding work alone.
